id_and_class.summary: David Rosenthal holds that a mental state is conscious when its subject has a higher-order thought that he or she is in that state, a thought that need not itself be conscious and does not seem to rest on inference. Mental qualities such as the redness of a sensation exist whether or not they are conscious; Rosenthal explains them separately, by how they map the perceptible properties we can discriminate.
id_and_class.core_identity_tagline: Consciousness as Thought About One’s Own States

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: A state’s being conscious consists in the subject being aware of it by way of a suitable higher-order thought that one is in that state.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: Mental states, their qualities, and the higher-order thoughts that make them conscious are all natural states of the organism; Rosenthal expects neural correlates of consciousness to be whatever mechanism produces the higher-order awareness.
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Weak emergence (consciousness is a relational property a state gains when targeted by a higher-order thought)
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: Subjectivity is the way we are aware of our own states, and the higher-order thought must not seem to rely on inference or observation, which captures the immediacy of that awareness. Intentionality belongs to first-order states and to the thoughts about them.
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: Mental qualities are fixed by their role in perceptual discrimination and occupy a ‘quality space’ that mirrors the similarities among perceptible properties. Because these qualities do not depend on consciousness, a sensation can have qualitative character without being conscious, as in subliminal perception.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: First-order mental states with qualitative and intentional properties, higher-order thoughts about them, and structure-preserving mappings between mental qualities and perceptible properties.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: Consciousness is known through our ordinary awareness of our own states, which needs no deliberate introspection; qualities are studied through what a subject can discriminate.
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: Two levels: first-order states (sensations, thoughts) and higher-order thoughts that represent the subject as being in them. Qualities sit in a quality space defined by discrimination.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: State consciousness (what makes a mental state conscious), qualitative character, and the difference between conscious and unconscious states.
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: A non-inferential higher-order thought that one is in a given state, which makes that first-order state conscious even when the thought itself is unconscious.
mechanism_and_dynamics.dynamics_of_emergence: A state becomes conscious when a suitable higher-order thought about it occurs and stays unconscious otherwise; deliberate introspection happens only when the higher-order thought is itself conscious.
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: First-order states represent perceptible properties through a homomorphism between quality space and the structure of the world. Higher-order thoughts represent the subject as being in those first-order states.
core_claims_and_evidence: A theory of consciousness must say what distinguishes conscious from unconscious states, and first-order theories such as Dretske’s and Block’s fail to explain why their preferred feature makes that difference.
No state counts as conscious unless one is in some way aware of it, so higher-order awareness is part of what being conscious means rather than an extra ingredient.
Mental qualities can be identified by their role in perceptual discrimination without any appeal to consciousness, which disarms puzzles such as undetectable quality inversion.
Higher-order theory constrains the search for neural correlates, since any correlate should point to a mechanism that produces higher-order awareness.
mechanism_and_dynamics.basis_of_belief_or_evidence_type: Philosophical, based on conceptual analysis of what it is for a state to be conscious, with links to perceptual discrimination and neuroscience.

empirics_and_critiques.criticisms_and_tensions: First-order theorists argue that higher-order awareness is an unneeded extra ingredient, and deflationists say being aware of a conscious state is like ‘smiling a smile’. Rosenthal replies that a deflated awareness cannot explain the contrast between conscious and unconscious states.
empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: Separating qualities from consciousness means the theory must explain what it is like to have a quality only through the higher-order thought, and the neural mechanism of higher-order awareness remains to be identified.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: Consistent with physicalism and functionalism; the split between quality theory and HOT theory keeps each part naturalistic.

AI_consciousness.rationale: Since consciousness depends on having suitable higher-order thoughts about one’s own states, a system able to form such thoughts would meet the condition in principle.

survival_beyond_death.rationale: Conscious states are natural states of an organism, so nothing remains conscious once those states stop occurring.

meaning_and_purpose.rationale: The theory is a naturalistic account of mental states and carries no cosmic purpose.

virtual_immortality.rationale: If the relevant first-order states and higher-order thoughts were reproduced, the view gives no principled reason the copy would lack consciousness.

sources_and_references.title_with_names: Rosenthal’s Higher-Order Thought, Landscape of Consciousness, David Rosenthal
